strengths: Novel theoretical insights: Lemma 4.1 provides clear geometric explanation of OOD leakage in prior-anchored perturbation; Proposition 1 establishes forward-KL upper bound on OOD probability with sound proofs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 task variants with 5 seeds, multiple OOD detectors (1-NN, LOF, Mahalanobis), thorough ablations, and runtime analysis demonstrating negligible overhead
Addresses real gap: First work combining expressive generative policies (diffusion/flow) with CVaR in offline risk-aware RL
Clear presentation: Well-motivated problem, effective visualizations (especially 2D bandit), extensive appendix with implementation details and hyperparameters enabling reproducibility
Insightful analysis: Connection between BC regularization and OOD control is novel and could influence future work; 2D synthetic task effectively illustrates geometric phenomena
weaknesses: Mixed empirical results contradict central claims: Hopper-Medium-Expert shows catastrophic failure (CVaR₀.₁ = -167.29 vs ORAAC 374.63; mean return -279.97) inadequately explained; claims of 'consistent gains' are misleading

Theory-practice gap: Bounds are proposition-level only, lack finite-sample guarantees; absolute continuity assumption may not hold with neural networks; CVaR degradation bound is loose and requires unknown Zmin, Zmax; no convergence analysis for RADAC itself
Limited algorithmic novelty: Core contribution (adding CVaR term to BC loss on diffusion policy) is incremental combination of existing components (IQN, diffusion policies, CVaR optimization)

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: Risk weight η differs dramatically (RADAC 0.05 vs RAFMAC 1000, 20× difference); limited guidance on when to use which α; no comparison to risk-neutral methods with aggressive tuning

Technical gaps: Lemma 4.1 assumes density lower bound c persists during training without justification; no convergence guarantees for critic updates with current policy bootstrapping; fixed τ grid may miss important quantiles

strengths: Addresses relevant problem of combining expressive multimodal policies with risk-aversion in offline RL
Comprehensive experimental suite including 2D synthetic task for intuition and systematic ablations
Honest discussion of limitations and practical constraints (Appendix A)
Good presentation of main motivation and clear problem formulation
Reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters and promised code release
Geometric analysis of prior-anchored perturbation limitations (Lemma 4.1) provides useful intuition
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines established components (BC regularization, IQN critics, CVaR objectives, diffusion/flow policies); concurrent works (refs 28, 51) perform similar combinations

Critical implementation-theory mismatch: Proposition 1 analyzes explicit likelihood log π_θ(a|s), but implementation uses denoising/velocity-matching losses (different optimization targets). Footnote 2 glosses over this fundamental discrepancy, undermining theoretical justification for BC regularization

Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 provides loose forward-KL upper bound with unverified practical tightness; Lemma 4.1's geometric insight is relatively straightforward and intuitive; no finite-sample or high-probability guarantees (acknowledged in limitations)

Unconvincing experimental results: (1) Table 1 shows highly inconsistent performance across tasks (RADAC fails badly on Hopper-m-e with CVaR -167.29 vs ORAAC 374.63); (2) Claim of 'consistent gains in CVaR0.1' not supported by data; (3) Table 3 (fixed 1000-step evaluation) shows worse results with extremely high variance (e.g., Hopper-m-e: -764.93±741.86 mean), suggesting main table cherry-picks checkpoints

Inadequate analysis of CVaR backpropagation through multi-step generative processes: Gradient variance and vanishing/exploding gradients through T=5 diffusion/K=10 flow steps not analyzed; 'full-path backprop' issues mentioned in limitations but not addressed

Hyperparameter sensitivity poorly explained: η differs by ~20x between RADAC (0.05) and RAFMAC (1000); Figures 7-9 show policy highly sensitive to η; different values needed per instantiation suggests method lacks robustness

Weak baseline comparisons: (1) ORAAC significantly outperforms RADAC on Hopper-m-e (CVaR 374.63 vs -167.29)—failure of the proposed method not explained; (2) Limited to locomotion domain; (3) No comparison with other recent risk-sensitive methods beyond ORAAC/CODAC

2D bandit evaluation limited in scope: Synthetic task specifically designed to highlight prior methods' failures; doesn't validate insights transfer to high-dimensional control where RADAC doesn't consistently outperform baselines
High variance and instability in results: Large standard errors (e.g., Walker2d-m-e: 689.32±) make conclusions unreliable; suggests method may be unstable in practice

OOD rate reduction (Table 2) doesn't translate to consistent performance gains: RADAC achieves lower OOD rates than ORAAC but doesn't consistently outperform on CVaR/mean, suggesting OOD rate alone insufficient for safety

strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: Lemma 4.1 provides geometric insight into why prior-anchored perturbation methods incur OOD actions; Proposition 1 establishes a principled forward-KL upper bound linking behavior regularization to OOD control

Comprehensive experimental validation including well-designed 2D synthetic task that effectively visualizes theoretical insights, thorough ablations (CVaR estimator variance, risk distortions, OOD detector robustness), and multiple evaluation protocols
Clear positioning and motivation addressing genuine gap in literature: expressive policies lack risk-awareness while risk-aware methods sacrifice expressiveness
Practical algorithm with minimal computational overhead relative to baselines; both diffusion (RADAC) and flow-matching (RAFMAC) variants provided
Well-written presentation with effective visualizations and logical progression from theory to experiments; honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Mixed and inconsistent empirical results undermine claims of 'consistent gains': RADAC shows catastrophic failures on Hopper tasks (CVaR=-167.29 vs ORAAC=374.63 on Hopper-m-e; -764.93 vs 660.07 on Hopper-m-e at 1000-step eval), and doesn't consistently dominate on both metrics across the 6 tasks evaluated
Inadequate analysis of failure modes: paper does not explain why RADAC fails on Hopper variants or provide guidance on when the method is expected to succeed, limiting practical utility

Limited theoretical scope: Proposition 1 requires β ≪ πθ (absolute continuity assumption that may not hold in practice); lacks finite-sample convergence guarantees or function approximation analysis; CVaR degradation bound is loose and doesn't account for distributional shift

Hyperparameter selection and tuning fairness concerns: critical parameter η differs 20x between RADAC (0.05) and RAFMAC (1000) without principled guidance; ORAAC/CODAC use 'authors' settings without sweeps' while others are swept; limited guidance on general η/K/N selection across domains

OOD detection methodology: 1-NN detector threshold κ=3 is arbitrary; ORAAC showing 65% OOD on HalfCheetah raises realism questions; Mahalanobis detector gives 0% OOD for ORAAC on Hopper, undermining confidence in OOD metrics despite attribution to 'detector limitations'

Limited evaluation scope: only locomotion tasks evaluated; Stochastic-D4RL is task-specific modification; unclear generalization to other risk-sensitive benchmarks or domains (manipulation, navigation, etc.)

Insufficient differentiation from concurrent work: references [28, 51] also combine diffusion/flow with distributional critics; novelty relative to these works and whether theoretical insights are new unclear

Analysis of gradient flow through long generative paths missing: backpropagating CVaR through full diffusion/flow trajectory could introduce high variance, but this is mentioned only as acknowledged limitation without empirical analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates the tension between safety and expressiveness in offline risk-aware RL with a compelling research question

Solid theoretical analysis: Lemma 4.1 on geometric limitations of prior-anchored perturbation, Lemma 4.2 linking KL divergence to OOD bounds, and Propositions 4.3-4.4 showing CVaR amplification under distribution shift provide useful intuitions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: thoughtfully designed 2D toy task illustrating geometric mechanisms, extensive Stochastic-D4RL benchmarks with multiple seeds, detailed ablations (objective components, risk distortions, tail sample size), OOD detector robustness validation with three detectors
Modular and simple design: composite objective L_π = L_BC + η L_Risk is straightforward to implement and works with any differentiable generative policy

Strong visualizations and presentation: Figure 3 (toy bandit) and Figure 10 (Pareto frontiers) effectively communicate method behavior; generally clear writing with detailed implementation specifications
Empirical OOD validation: Table 2 demonstrates lower out-of-distribution action rates for RADAC compared to ORAAC variants, consistent with theoretical predictions
weaknesses: Limited theoretical guarantees: lacks finite-sample convergence analysis, high-probability bounds under function approximation, and sample complexity comparisons; Proposition 4.3 bounds rely on bounded utility [m, M] with unclear practical tightness; theory is descriptive rather than prescriptive

Mixed experimental results: RADAC underperforms FQL on mean return in several tasks (Table 1: Walker2d-m-r, Hopper-m-r); CVaR improvements are sometimes marginal with high variance (Table 3); fixed-checkpoint results (Table 3) show RAFMAC sometimes outperforming RADAC, suggesting checkpoint selection bias in main results

Hyperparameter sensitivity and design concerns: risk weight η varies 20× between RADAC (0.05) and RAFMAC (1000) with no principled selection method; BC weight fixed at 1.0; task-specific target return clipping ([-300,300]) appears necessary but somewhat contradicts claims of avoiding extra regularization; non-standard midpoint quadrature for CVaR estimation raises reproducibility concerns

Limited scope of evaluation: restricted to MuJoCo locomotion with artificial Bernoulli penalty hazards; no higher-dimensional action spaces, vision-based tasks, or realistic safety constraints; primary evaluation on CVaR₀.₁ only with limited exploration of other risk levels

Insufficient analysis of OOD-CVaR connection: while Table 2 shows lower OOD rates, the causal link to CVaR performance is not rigorously established; Lemma 4.1 is conditional (doesn't prove prior-anchored perturbation fails in practice); thin/nonconvex support assumption not always valid for learned D4RL policies

Concurrent work and novelty concerns: Liu et al. (2025) and Zhang et al. (2025a) also combine diffusion with distributional critics; RAMAC's novelty is primarily optimizing CVaR along the generative path with BC, which is somewhat incremental; delineation from concurrent work is unclear

CVaR estimator quality not analyzed: critic inaccuracy early in training could provide poor CVaR gradients; Figure 12 shows non-negligible estimator variance even at K=16; impact on gradient quality unexplored; relationship between critic convergence and policy performance not examined

Missing experimental details and comparisons: no systematic hyperparameter sweep for η across tasks; limited exploration of alternative risk objectives; OOD detection uses somewhat arbitrary thresholds (k=10, κ=3); project website URL not provided for reproducibility

strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed empirical study with 12 tasks, multiple baseline comparisons, and extensive appendix material demonstrating reproducibility
Clear geometric intuition via Lemma 4.1 and 2D toy bandit effectively illustrating limitations of anchor-perturbation methods on nonconvex supports
Consistent CVaR improvements across most benchmarks (Table 1); practical modular framework requiring no extra learned components (no ensembles/dynamics models)
Thorough implementation documentation with detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, multiple OOD detectors for validation, and promised code release
Honest discussion of limitations and acknowledgment of concurrent similar work (Liu et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2025a)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines three existing ideas (expressive generative policies, CVaR, BC) in straightforward manner; concurrent work (Liu et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2025a) pursues very similar directions, weakening contribution claim

Weak theoretical contribution: Lemma 4.2 bounds are intuitive (BC suppresses OOD), Prop 4.3 shows known 1/α CVaR amplification; no finite-sample convergence guarantees or surprising insights; gap between claimed KL analysis and actual diffusion/flow BC surrogates not rigorously addressed

Mixed empirical results with unclear statistical significance: Table 1 shows inconsistent mean-return wins; error bars often overlap; Table 3 (fixed-checkpoint evaluation) contradicts main-paper conclusions with different algorithm rankings; RAFMAC sometimes outperforms RADAC

Artificial experimental setup: Stochastic-D4RL uses Bernoulli penalties tied to thresholds rather than realistic failure modes; evaluation limited to MuJoCo locomotion only; fixed CVaR level α=0.1 with limited sensitivity analysis

Insufficient ablation of design choices: no justification for L_π = L_BC + η L_CVaR form vs alternatives; unclear value of multimodality if BC constrains to data manifold; wild η variation (RADAC: 0.05 vs RAFMAC: 1000) unexplained; limited analysis of BC-CVaR interaction during training

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem combining expressiveness with safety in offline RL, filling a genuine gap between risk-neutral expressive methods and risk-aware restricted policies
Theoretically sound framework with correct proofs; Lemma 4.1 provides valuable geometric insight into why prior-anchored perturbation can retain OOD leakage
Lemma 4.2 and Proposition 4.3/Corollary 4.4 formalize the connection between behavior divergence control and CVaR stability, though with known bounds
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 task-dataset combinations with consistent CVaR improvements (Table 1) and empirically validated OOD action suppression (Table 2, 6) using multiple detectors
Excellent pedagogical 2D bandit visualization (Figure 3) clearly demonstrates geometric mechanisms and superiority over prior-anchored and risk-neutral baselines

Strong experimental practices: multiple complementary baselines, extensive ablations (BC vs CVaR roles, risk distortions, quantile sample sizes), multiple evaluation protocols (standard and fixed-checkpoint)
Thorough reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters (Table 7), implementation details (Appendix D), multiple OOD detector specifications, 5 seeds per experiment
Honest limitations discussion in Appendix A; appropriately scopes claims and acknowledges lack of finite-sample guarantees under function approximation
Simple, modular, and practical framework (Algorithm 1) that practitioners can readily implement; comparable computational cost to baselines (Section E.4)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is relatively straightforward application of CVaR gradient backprop through generative policies with BC regularization; both behavior-regularized methods and distributional RL for risk are well-established

Theory-practice gap: Lemma 4.2 assumes forward KL (log-likelihood), but RADAC/RAFMAC use native BC surrogates (denoising/flow-matching losses) that don't exactly correspond to log-likelihood; footnote acknowledges but doesn't formally connect

Theoretical results are somewhat incremental: Proposition 4.3's 1/α amplification of CVaR under TV distance is relatively unsurprising; paper doesn't explore when this bound becomes vacuous for small α or analyze scaling with (M-m)

Mixed empirical results across all metrics: CVaR improvements consistent but not dominant on all tasks; FQL often achieves competitive or superior mean returns; Table 3 (fixed-checkpoint) shows less consistent improvements
Paper doesn't adequately explain underperformance in some settings (e.g., why DiffusionQL outperforms on some Walker2d variants in Table 3) or when RAMAC is preferred

Artificial experimental setup: Stochastic hazards use simple Bernoulli penalties with task-specific thresholds; not reflective of realistic continuous risk or state-dependent hazards; early termination logic varies across tasks

Concurrent related work exists (Liu et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2025a pairing diffusion with distributional critics); differentiation is primarily implementation-level (CVaR backprop vs fixed critic signals), limiting novelty

Incomplete theoretical scope: no finite-sample convergence rates or sample complexity analysis; analysis doesn't account for function approximation or partial dataset coverage; Lemma 4.1 condition (density ≥ c on leakage region) may be difficult to verify in practice
Missing analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity: main results use fixed α=0.1; only limited α-sweep on toy task (Figure 9); interaction between BC and CVaR weights not fully explored

Notation and presentation could be clearer: π vs ψ distinction, Zϕ quantiles vs Zπ distribution; key implementation detail (quantile grid via midpoint quadrature) relegated to appendix; project website URL not provided in review version
